name: Dag Nasty
label: Dischord
lede: Brian Baker walked out of Minor Threat with songs that wanted a melody, and Dag Nasty got three singers in two years while making Can I Say, the record people still point to.

eras.title: Minor Threat's guitarist wants a melody
eras.text: Minor Threat was done, and Brian Baker had songs faster than pop and catchier than hardcore was allowing itself. He pulled a rhythm section out of Bloody Mannequin Orchestra and a singer out of the D.C. scene, and by Halloween they had a whole album on tape.

yt: Live at WUST Radio Music Hall, 1985
years.h: Baker pulls a band out of Bloody Mannequin Orchestra
years.p: Drummer [[Colin Sears|c9bbc03c-06bf-4c37-9f54-e95b51aede4c]] and bassist [[Roger Marbury|c24bb563-e743-4478-9380-fe877ca4031f]] come over from Bloody Mannequin Orchestra and [[Shawn Brown|e39556a4-0d8f-4138-bc18-a54d3a66eefe]] sings. Brian Baker, ex-[[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]], has the songs.

eras.title: Smalley sings one record, then leaves
eras.text: Can I Say, the record that made Dag Nasty's name, came together fast with Boston singer Dave Smalley, who wasn't staying. By the end of 1986 the band had lost him, toured half the country with Peter Cortner, found through a classified ad, and quit.

yt: Live at Chevy Chase Community Center, March 21, 1986
years.h: Boston shouter Dave Smalley replaces Shawn Brown
years.p: [[Dave Smalley|c637a12d-5f55-4b83-bef0-a56b3c1e326c]] of the Boston straight-edge band [[DYS|f012c04d-96ca-47dd-9359-3bb11fed88b5]] takes the mic, and a hardcore screamer is suddenly fronting the most tuneful band in D.C.

years.h: The Electric Banana in Pittsburgh rolls tape
years.p: Dag Nasty's show at the Pittsburgh club is recorded. Four live tracks from that night later ride along as bonus cuts on the Can I Say CD.

years.h: Can I Say arrives as Dischord No. 19, chorus pedal and all
years.p: Recut at Inner Ear with Ian MacKaye producing and Dave Smalley singing. Baker's MXR chorus pedal, found lying around the studio, ends up all over it.
years.xp:
Baker played a '70s Les Paul goldtop through a Marshall. Eight of the songs had been around since the Shawn Brown session. He told Guitar World he went in thinking: "We need a couple ragers that sound like Minor Threat."

The borrowed chorus pedal is the secret ingredient, the wide ringing sheen that set the record apart from the D.C. hardcore around it. For touring, Baker swapped it for a Boss CE-3000 Super Chorus.

The album's reach runs long. Its songs are cited in histories of emo, Circles turned up on a Tony Hawk game soundtrack, and Blink-182's Travis Barker has the title tattooed on his chest.

years.big: "Dave decides he's going to go do graduate school."
years.h: Smalley picks grad school over the Descendents tour
years.p: Dag Nasty have the opening slot on a huge summer run with the [[Descendents|f035837e-4117-438d-a524-cacf43500e68]]. Dave Smalley leaves before it starts for New York University, as Baker told Guitar World.
years.xp:
It was the break a young band waits for, and it came apart on the calendar. Smalley chose school, and Brian Baker was left with dates on the books and nobody to sing them.

The fix was Peter Cortner, found through a classified ad, and his voice changed Dag Nasty's direction for the next two years.

years.h: A want ad turns up Peter Cortner
years.p: Dag Nasty places an ad in a local paper and finds [[Peter Cortner|66e99d7d-3c1e-429b-a95c-5591f9278616]]. He learns the set and tours with the Descendents across half the United States.

years.h: Home from the road, Dag Nasty quit
years.p: After the Descendents tour and a few local shows the band calls it. Baker heads to Los Angeles and starts Doggy Style with Descendents bassist [[Doug Carrion|bdc25394-8356-4bcd-9118-520f17af9333]].

eras.title: Cortner's voice, and a pop turn
eras.text: Baker and Doug Carrion rebuilt Dag Nasty around Cortner, which pushed the band further toward pop. That made two albums, Wig Out at Denko's and Field Day, a move off Dischord to Giant Records, and the end of the original run.

yt: Live at Fender's Ballroom, Long Beach, March 27, 1987
years.h: Baker restarts Dag Nasty with Doug Carrion on bass
years.p: Brian Baker, Peter Cortner and Colin Sears are joined by Carrion, and Roger Marbury declines to come back.

years.h: Cortner's first record is Wig Out at Denko's, Dischord No. 26
years.p: Dag Nasty's second album, recorded at Inner Ear in March with Ian MacKaye and Don Zientara: brighter, poppier, still fast. Alternative Press later put it in the emo canon.
years.xp: The title is a D.C. in-joke: the band's own site says Denko was a guy from Washington who threw house parties.

years.h: All Ages Show 7" goes to Giant
years.p: A single for Giant Records, the label that would put out the next album, Field Day.

years.h: Colin Sears is out, and Scott Garrett drums on Field Day
years.p: Founding drummer Colin Sears is gone by the time Dag Nasty cuts its third album for Giant. [[Scott Garrett|0e8c8d56-4adf-450c-bcb9-367940a25a6d]] plays on it.

years.h: Field Day goes to Giant with a Ruts cover
years.p: Pop hooks, hardcore speed, a cover of [[The Ruts|a2f938aa-1aa3-474b-a070-762067274eab]] and a remake of Under Your Influence from Can I Say. It's the band's third and most ambitious album.
years.xp: Robert Christgau gave it an A minus. According to Wikipedia, it sold more than 30,000 copies in its first year.

years.h: Dag Nasty's first run ends after the Field Day tour
years.p: By the band's own count, four years produced three singers, two bass players and three drummers.
years.xp: In 2009 Brian Baker was still calling Peter Cortner a really good lyricist and talking about another record with him.

eras.title: Dale Nixon plays guitar
eras.text: Baker went off to play hard rock in Junkyard and signed a contract that followed him back to punk. The Can I Say line-up made one more album anyway, Four on the Floor, with Baker credited as Dale Nixon. Then he joined Bad Religion, and stayed.

years.h: Baker turns to hard rock with Junkyard
years.p: Brian Baker and Chris Gates, formerly of Austin's Big Boys, start the Los Angeles band [[Junkyard|0388b116-a688-4122-bfb7-ca9a1f4aef1a]]. It's a long way from Inner Ear.

years.h: Selfless Records digs up 85-86
years.p: Selfless puts out a set of Dag Nasty's recordings from before Can I Say.

years.h: Four on the Floor credits Baker as Dale Nixon
years.p: Dave Smalley, Roger Marbury and Colin Sears return on Epitaph, cut in Los Angeles in summer 1991 with [[Brett Gurewitz|cd40188b-ea30-4729-bebb-e8c5091c9d02]] producing. Baker hides behind the alias because Junkyard has him under contract.
years.xp:
Dale Nixon is a punk in-joke with a history: it's the alias Greg Ginn used for his bass parts on [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]]'s My War. Baker borrowing it for a contractual workaround is about as DC-to-LA as a credit line gets.

The Washington Post called the album first-rate. It was the Can I Say band, minus Baker's name on the sleeve.

years.h: Baker turns down R.E.M. for Bad Religion
years.p: Brian Baker passes on a touring spot with R.E.M. and takes Brett Gurewitz's place in [[Bad Religion|149e6720-4e4a-41a4-afca-6d29083fc091]]. Three decades on, he's still there.

eras.title: Back to the basement
eras.text: Dag Nasty came home to Inner Ear for a full-length that sounded like hardcore again. Then Dischord opened the vault on the session that started everything.

years.h: Smalley sings again on Minority of One
years.p: Recorded at Inner Ear with Don Zientara and ex-Minor Threat bassist [[Steve Hansgen|cd469927-13a8-4d0b-8898-01c6856f5878]] producing, and the tempos go back up. Drowned in Sound liked it; Pitchfork didn't.

years.cap: Shawn Brown singing with Dag Nasty at the Black Cat, Washington, D.C., December 28, 2012
years.h: Dag With Shawn, a 1985 session nobody heard for 25 years
years.p: Dag Nasty cut nine songs with Shawn Brown at Inner Ear on Halloween 1985, then shelved them when Brown left. Dischord restored the master tapes and released them as No. 168.
years.xp:
[[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] produced the session in Don Zientara's Arlington basement. Dischord's notes say the album was shelved after Brown departed, and in early 1986 the band recut it with Dave Smalley as Can I Say.

Brown went on to front [[Swiz|eea2f3d8-1e94-436c-ae66-4633f99f55be]], one of the harder-edged D.C. bands of the next few years, and came back to Dag Nasty on his own terms in 2012.

eras.title: The first singer gets his turn
eras.text: The original line-up with Shawn Brown, once a footnote, became a working band. The D.C. punk documentary Salad Days got them on stage, and a new session at Inner Ear gave Brown his first Dag Nasty release that didn't come out of the archive.

years.cap: Shawn Brown fronting Dag Nasty at the Black Cat, Washington, D.C., December 28, 2012
years.h: The original four finally play a show together
years.p: Shawn Brown, Brian Baker, Roger Marbury and Colin Sears, announced in October as their first show together since 1985, play D.C.'s Black Cat for the Salad Days: The DC Punk Revolution benefit. [[Government Issue|9b952ee8-d45d-4a26-8066-57849d871e06]] are on the bill too.

years.cap: Dag Nasty at Auditorium Shores, Austin, November 2015
years.h: Cold Heart: Shawn Brown's first new songs with the band
years.p: The original four record Cold Heart and Wanting Nothing at Inner Ear in December 2015 with Ian MacKaye and Don Zientara. Dischord releases them as No. 184, three decades after Smalley replaced Brown.

years.cap: Dag Nasty at SO36, Berlin, April 28, 2016
years.h: Dag Nasty spend spring 2016 on the road
years.p: A European run, Punk Rock Bowling in Las Vegas, and a June 11 date in Asbury Park, New Jersey.

years.h: Live at the Black Cat, April 21, 2016
yt: Live at the Black Cat, April 21, 2016
